theorem.statement:
Fix deterministic total orders on the encoded finite sets.  The dominance-and-symmetry handle admits the following exact resolution.  There is a deterministic exact-rational generator which, on every rational instance, returns a finite certificate \(\mathsf{Cert}=(S^{\star},v^{\star},\mathcal T)\) accepted by the independently executed map \(\mathsf{Check}\); acceptance certifies \(v^{\star}=\overline W(S^{\star})=D^{\star}\).  The generator enumerates \(\mathcal P_k\) to obtain its incumbent and then branches on the least undecided candidate, closing a node \((I,E,O)\) exactly when \(|I|>k\) or \(\overline W(I\cup E)\geq v^{\star}\).  Thus it always terminates, although its tree can be exponential.

For every rational instance with \(|\mathcal X|=3\) and \(|\mathcal C|\leq5\), the generator, exhaustive panel enumeration, and the fixed-selection values of \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{MILP}}\) agree exactly on the optimum and on the complete set of minimizing panels; with the same deterministic tie rule they return the same panel.  In particular, on \(\mathsf E_{3,5}\) the exact value is \(1/8\), the minimizing panels are \(\{c_1,c_4\}\) and \(\{c_2,c_3\}\), and \(\mathsf{Check}(\{c_1,c_4\},1/8,\mathcal T_{3,5})=\mathrm{true}\).

Moreover, the following nontrivial, computable structural condition on the action-score cost tensor guarantees a polynomial certificate:
\[
 \text{there exists }S_0\in\mathcal P_k\text{ such that }
 \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S_0\}\bigr)
 =\min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in\mathcal C\}\bigr)
 \quad\text{for every }(\pi,x)\in\mathcal F\times\mathcal X. \tag{SC}
\]
Under \(\mathrm{(SC)}\), the generated branch tree consists only of the root.  A sufficient condition checkable with \(O(|\mathcal F||\mathcal X||\mathcal C|)\) rational comparisons is that the union of one fixed tie-broken minimizing candidate for every pair \((\pi,x)\) whose full-library minimum is strictly below the dummy cost \(1\) has cardinality at most \(k\).  The one-node tree and its incumbent have encoding length polynomial in the rational input length.  This finite completeness and structural compression do not assert a polynomial-time exact generator on unrestricted instances; such a generator would, by the stated NP-hardness reduction, imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Define, for every \(S\subseteq\mathcal C\), the exact rational objective
\[
 g(S)=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}
       \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}q_x
       \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S\}\bigr).
 \tag{1}
\]
The sets \(\mathcal X\), \(\mathcal C\), and \(\mathcal F\) are finite, \(\mathcal F\) is nonempty, and all \(q_x\) and \(d_{\pi xc}\) are rational by the definitions of the cell weights and score costs.  Hence every minimum, sum, and maximum in (1) is attained and can be evaluated by exact rational arithmetic.  Although the displayed width theorem is phrased for a budget-feasible panel, its width assertion applies to every subset of \(\mathcal C\): for a given \(S\subseteq\mathcal C\), instantiate that theorem with the auxiliary budget \(k'=|\mathcal C|\).  Then \(S\in\mathcal P_{k'}\), while neither \(g(S)\) nor the defining expression for \(\overline W(S)\) contains the budget.  The width identity therefore gives
\[
 g(S)=\overline W(S)                                                       \tag{2}
\]
for every \(S\subseteq\mathcal C\).  Since
\(\mathcal P_k=\{S\subseteq\mathcal C:|S|\leq k\}\) is finite and nonempty (it contains \(\varnothing\)), exact enumeration yields
\[
 v^{\star}:=\min_{S\in\mathcal P_k}g(S)=D^{\star}.                       \tag{3}
\]
Let \(S^{\star}\) be the first minimizer in the fixed order.  Equations (2)--(3) give
\[
 S^{\star}\in\mathcal P_k,
 \qquad
 g(S^{\star})=\overline W(S^{\star})=v^{\star}.                          \tag{4}
\]

We now construct the tree, rather than assume its existence.  Begin with the root
\((I,E,O)=(\varnothing,\mathcal C,\varnothing)\).  At a current node, make it a leaf if
\[
 |I|>k
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 g(I\cup E)\geq v^{\star}.                                                \tag{5}
\]
If neither test succeeds, then \(E\neq\varnothing\).  Indeed, if \(E=\varnothing\), failure of the first test gives \(I\in\mathcal P_k\), while failure of the second and (3) give the contradiction
\[
 g(I)<v^{\star}=\min_{S\in\mathcal P_k}g(S)\leq g(I).                     \tag{6}
\]
Thus the least element \(c\in E\) exists.  Give the node exactly the two children
\[
 (I\cup\{c\},E\setminus\{c\},O)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 (I,E\setminus\{c\},O\cup\{c\}).                                      \tag{7}
\]
At each passage to a child, \(|E|\) falls by one.  Consequently every path has length at most \(|\mathcal C|\); (6) shows that a path with \(E=\varnothing\) must have closed, so the construction produces a finite binary tree with at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|+1}-1\) nodes.  The root, partitions, children, and leaf conditions in (5)--(7) are exactly those in the certificate grammar, with (2) identifying the second quantity in (5) as the checker's optimistic-descendant bound \(\overline W(I\cup E)\).

The checker receives only the rational instance and the resulting certificate.  It independently recomputes the left side of (4) from (1), verifies every set partition and both children in (7), and recomputes every leaf value in (5); it need not trust (3) or the generator's search log.  Therefore all of its Boolean tests succeed.  The certificate soundness theorem then yields
\[
 \mathsf{Check}(\mathsf{Cert})=\mathrm{true}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \overline W(S^{\star})=v^{\star}=D^{\star},                             \tag{8}
\]
which proves both exact soundness and finite completeness of this instantiation of \(\mathsf{Handle}\).  Checking one node requires at most \(O(|\mathcal F||\mathcal X||\mathcal C|)\) rational comparisons and additions in (1), besides linear-size set checks.  Thus verification time is polynomial in the input and displayed-certificate lengths; exact integer numerators and denominators have bit lengths polynomial in the rational input length under these finitely many minima and sums.

For the bounded audit, if \(|\mathcal C|\leq5\), there are at most
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{k}{|\mathcal C|\choose j}\leq2^5=32                       \tag{9}
\]
feasible panels.  The generator and a separately written exhaustive enumerator therefore evaluate the same finite list by the same mathematical map (1), using no rounding.  For a fixed integral selection vector, the mixed-integer equivalence theorem says that minimizing its \(b\)-variables assigns every \((\pi,x)\) to a cheapest selected column or to the dummy column.  Its value is consequently exactly (1).  Hence enumeration and all fixed-selection mixed-integer values agree panel by panel, and minimizing them gives the same objective and minimizer set.  This proves the assertion for every three-cell instance with at most five candidates; the number three is not needed for the equality, but fixes the requested audit class.

For completeness, direct substitution for \(\mathsf E_{3,5}\), in the order consisting of the empty panel, the five singletons, and the ten lexicographically ordered pairs, gives the exact worst-width list
\[
 1;quad
 \frac78,\frac58,\frac78,\frac58,1;quad
 \frac12,\frac12,\frac18,\frac78,\frac18,
 \frac16,\frac58,\frac12,\frac58,\frac38.                              \tag{10}
\]
Thus the minimum in (10) is \(1/8\), attained exactly at
\(\{c_1,c_4\}\) and \(\{c_2,c_3\}\).  The exact three-cell audit further verifies each coordinatewise cost calculation, the fixed-selection mixed-integer value, and every leaf of \(\mathcal T_{3,5}\); hence
\[
 \operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{MILP}})=\frac18,
 \qquad
 \mathsf{Check}(\{c_1,c_4\},1/8,\mathcal T_{3,5})=\mathrm{true}.         \tag{11}
\]
Equations (10)--(11) are therefore an exact early-kill comparison, not a floating-point solver receipt.

It remains to prove the compression claim.  Suppose \(S_0\) satisfies \(\mathrm{(SC)}\).  Applying the positive weights and then the maximum over \(\pi\) to the equalities in \(\mathrm{(SC)}\) gives
\[
 g(S_0)=g(\mathcal C).                                                     \tag{12}
\]
For every \(S\subseteq\mathcal C\), enlarging the set over which a minimum is taken cannot increase that minimum.  Hence, coordinate by coordinate,
\[
 \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S\}\bigr)
 \geq
 \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in\mathcal C\}\bigr),          \tag{13}
\]
and the nonnegative weighted sums and maximum in (1) preserve (13), so
\[
 g(S)\geq g(\mathcal C).                                                   \tag{14}
\]
Since \(S_0\in\mathcal P_k\), equations (3), (12), and (14) imply
\[
 g(\mathcal C)\leq v^{\star}\leq g(S_0)=g(\mathcal C),
 \qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad
 v^{\star}=g(\mathcal C).                                                 \tag{15}
\]
At the root, \(I\cup E=\mathcal C\), so (15) makes the second leaf test in (5) hold with equality.  The certificate tree therefore has exactly one node.  Its remaining data are the characteristic vector of \(S^{\star}\), the exact rational number \(v^{\star}\), and fixed-size delimiters; this has length polynomial in the full rational input encoding.

Finally, \(\mathrm{(SC)}\) itself has a direct computable sufficient test.  Put
\[
 \delta_{\pi x}:=
 \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in\mathcal C\}\bigr).            \tag{16}
\]
Whenever \(\delta_{\pi x}<1\), finiteness of \(\mathcal C\) implies that some candidate attains \(\delta_{\pi x}\); choose the least such candidate and take the union \(H\) of these choices over all \((\pi,x)\).  If \(\delta_{\pi x}<1\), the selected minimizer in \(H\) makes the minimum over \(H\) at most \(\delta_{\pi x}\), while \(H\subseteq\mathcal C\) makes it at least \(\delta_{\pi x}\).  If \(\delta_{\pi x}=1\), the dummy value \(1\) makes both minima equal to one.  Therefore
\[
 \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi x c}:c\in H\}\bigr)=\delta_{\pi x}
 \quad\text{for every }(\pi,x).                                         \tag{17}
\]
If \(|H|\leq k\), then \(H\in\mathcal P_k\), and (17) proves \(\mathrm{(SC)}\) with \(S_0=H\).  Computing (16), the tie-broken minimizers, and their union uses \(O(|\mathcal F||\mathcal X||\mathcal C|)\) rational comparisons.  This condition can hold with \(k<|\mathcal C|\), for example when duplicate columns or candidates that never attain a coordinatewise minimum are discarded, so it is a genuine cost-tensor restriction rather than the vacuous condition \(k\geq|\mathcal C|\).

The construction above makes no unrestricted polynomial-time claim: it explicitly permits the exponential bound preceding (8).  If an exact generator ran in polynomial time on every rational instance, reading its incumbent value would compute \(D^{\star}\) in polynomial time.  The frozen maximum-coverage reduction proves that this optimization is NP-hard even on its stated boundary subclass.  Thus such an unrestricted polynomial-time conclusion would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\); NP-hardness does not invalidate the one-node certificate under \(\mathrm{(SC)}\), nor does it by itself rule out short certificates on other subclasses.
